# Lighting Arrangement with Distance-Based Calibration and Control

## System Overview

The lighting arrangement disclosed herein comprises a lighting device configured with an adjustable luminous output, enabling dynamic control over the intensity or characteristics of the emitted light. This lighting device operates in conjunction with a control arrangement that is communicatively coupled to it, allowing for seamless data exchange and command execution. At the heart of this control arrangement is a controller responsible for adjusting the light output of the lighting device based on various operational parameters and inputs received during system operation.

## Calibration Data Storage

A key feature of the system is a data storage device that is accessible by the controller and serves as a repository for calibration data. This calibration data is specifically associated with a light measurement device incorporated within a mobile communication device, such as a smartphone or similar portable electronic device equipped with light-sensing capabilities. Importantly, the calibration data is structured as a function of the distance between the mobile communication device and the lighting device, meaning that for various distances, corresponding expected light measurement values are recorded and stored. This distance-dependent calibration profile forms the foundation upon which the system can later determine positional information based on measured light output.

## Communication and Measurement Process

To facilitate the distance determination process, the control arrangement employs a communication module that serves two primary functions. First, it instructs the lighting device to produce a predefined luminous output, establishing a known reference point for light emission. Second, this same communication module receives a luminous output measurement from a mobile communication device that is located somewhere within the vicinity of the lighting device, but at a distance that is not initially known to the system. The mobile device, using its integrated light measurement device, captures the intensity or characteristics of the light emitted by the lighting device and transmits this measurement back to the control arrangement.

## Distance Determination

Upon receiving the luminous output measurement from the mobile communication device, the system performs a comparison operation, matching the received measurement against the previously stored calibration data. Since the calibration data correlates specific light measurement values with corresponding distances, this comparison process allows the system to retrieve distance information that accurately indicates how far the mobile communication device is positioned from the lighting device. This retrieval process effectively transforms a light intensity measurement into meaningful spatial information without requiring additional dedicated distance-sensing hardware.

## Adaptive Light Output Adjustment

Once the distance information has been retrieved, the controller utilizes this data to adjust the luminous output of the lighting device accordingly. This adjustment may be performed to achieve various objectives, such as maintaining a consistent illumination level at the location of the mobile communication device, optimizing energy efficiency, or accommodating specific lighting requirements based on the determined distance. The closed-loop nature of this process—instructing output, measuring at the receiving device, retrieving distance, and adjusting output—enables the lighting system to dynamically respond to the position of mobile devices within its operational range.

## Additional Aspects of the Disclosure

Beyond the lighting arrangement itself, the present disclosure extends to encompass several related aspects. These include a computer program product configured to execute the necessary computational steps for calibration data comparison and distance retrieval, a mobile communication device specifically adapted to incorporate the light measurement device and communicate measurement data to the control arrangement, and a comprehensive lighting system that integrates the lighting device, control arrangement, and associated components into a unified, functional whole. Collectively, these elements provide a versatile solution for distance-aware lighting control applicable across a range of environments and use cases.

# Lighting Arrangement for Distance-Based Illumination Control

## Background and Technical Challenge

Modern lighting systems increasingly rely on mobile communication devices—such as smartphones or tablets—to provide personalized and context-aware illumination. However, an important technical challenge arises in these interactive lighting environments: determining the precise, unknown distance between a mobile device and a dimmable lighting device without resorting to additional dedicated distance-sensing hardware such as infrared sensors, ultrasonic transducers, or camera-based depth-sensing modules. Traditional approaches to distance measurement typically require the integration of specialized components, which adds cost, complexity, and potential points of failure to lighting systems that are otherwise designed to be simple and energy-efficient.

## Overview of the Solution

The lighting arrangement described here addresses this problem through an elegant, hardware-efficient methodology that leverages the light source itself as the medium for distance determination. Rather than depending on dedicated proximity sensors, the system utilizes a controller integrated with the dimmable lighting device to orchestrate a calibrated measurement process.

## Detailed Operation of the System

The process begins when the controller instructs the dimmable lighting device to produce a **predefined luminous output**—a known, specific light intensity level that serves as a reference point for subsequent calculations. This predefined output is deliberately controlled so that its characteristics are precisely known to the system in advance.

Once the lighting device emits this reference luminous output, the mobile communication device—equipped with a light sensor or ambient light detection capability—captures a **luminous output measurement**. This measurement reflects how much of the emitted light actually reaches the mobile device, which is directly influenced by the physical distance separating the two devices, following principles related to light intensity attenuation over distance.

The mobile device then transmits this measured luminous output value back to the controller, typically via a wireless communication protocol such as Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or another suitable short-range communication standard.

Upon receiving this luminous output measurement, the controller performs a critical lookup operation: it accesses **stored calibration data**—a pre-established dataset that maps specific luminous output measurements to corresponding distance values. This calibration data may have been generated during a setup or manufacturing phase, wherein known distances were paired with their resulting luminous output measurements under controlled conditions, thereby creating a reliable reference table or function.

By cross-referencing the received measurement against this calibration data, the controller can accurately **retrieve the corresponding distance information**, effectively determining how far the mobile device is positioned from the lighting device without any direct distance-sensing mechanism.

## Practical Application and Advantages

Once the distance has been calculated through this measurement-and-lookup process, the system can then intelligently **adjust the luminous output of the lighting device** based on the determined distance. For example, if the mobile device is detected to be far from the light source, the controller might increase the luminous intensity to maintain adequate illumination at that distance. Conversely, if the mobile device is very close, the system might reduce the output to prevent excessive brightness or to conserve energy.

This distance-aware adjustment capability offers several significant advantages:

1. **Cost Efficiency**: By eliminating the need for dedicated distance-sensing hardware (such as ultrasonic sensors, infrared rangefinders, or depth cameras), the overall system cost is substantially reduced.

2. **Simplified Design**: The lighting device and controller can maintain a simpler architecture, as they rely on components already present in typical lighting fixtures (light output control) and mobile devices (light sensors), rather than requiring additional specialized sensing modules.

3. **Reduced Complexity**: Fewer hardware components generally translate to improved reliability and easier maintenance, as there are fewer potential points of mechanical or electronic failure.

4. **Energy Efficiency**: The distance-based adjustment allows the lighting system to optimize its output according to actual need, potentially reducing unnecessary energy consumption when full luminous intensity is not required based on the proximity of the user's device.

5. **Scalability**: This calibration-based approach can be readily adapted to various lighting devices and environments, as the calibration data can be customized to reflect the specific characteristics of different lighting installations, room configurations, or ambient conditions.

## Conclusion

In summary, this lighting arrangement provides an innovative and resource-efficient solution to the problem of distance determination in mobile-integrated lighting systems. By utilizing a controller that orchestrates the production of a known luminous output, receives corresponding measurements from a mobile device, and cross-references this data against pre-stored calibration information, the system achieves accurate distance estimation. This, in turn, enables sophisticated, distance-aware control of the lighting device's luminous output—all without the added expense, complexity, and potential failure points associated with dedicated distance-sensing hardware. This approach represents a practical and elegant solution for creating responsive, adaptive lighting environments that intelligently respond to user proximity.

# Disclosed Information: Understanding Its Meaning and Implications

The term "disclosed" refers to information that has been made known, revealed, or shared with relevant parties. Disclosure plays a critical role across numerous fields, including law, business, finance, medicine, and everyday communication, serving as a foundation for transparency and informed decision-making.

## The Concept of Disclosure

At its core, disclosure involves the deliberate act of sharing information that might otherwise remain hidden or private. This can range from a company revealing financial data to shareholders, to a doctor informing a patient about treatment risks, to an individual sharing personal information in a relationship. The act of disclosing something implies that prior to the disclosure, the information was not fully known or accessible to the receiving party.

## Legal and Business Contexts

In legal settings, disclosure requirements ensure fairness and accountability. Businesses are often legally obligated to disclose certain information to protect consumers, investors, and employees. For example:

- **Financial disclosures** require publicly traded companies to reveal earnings, risks, and material changes that could affect stock prices
- **Contractual disclosures** ensure all parties understand terms, conditions, and potential liabilities before signing agreements
- **Employment disclosures** may involve revealing workplace hazards, company policies, or conflicts of interest

Failure to disclose required information can result in legal consequences, including lawsuits, fines, or loss of licenses.

## Disclosure in Personal and Ethical Contexts

Beyond formal and legal settings, disclosure carries significant weight in personal relationships and ethical considerations. Trust often depends on what has and hasn't been disclosed. Withholding important information—even without malicious intent—can damage relationships or lead to unintended harm.

In journalism and research, disclosure of conflicts of interest is considered essential to maintaining credibility and public trust. Researchers, for instance, must disclose funding sources that might influence their findings.

## The Balance Between Disclosure and Privacy

While disclosure promotes transparency, it must be balanced against privacy rights and confidentiality concerns. Not all information warrants disclosure, and various frameworks—such as non-disclosure agreements (NDAs)—exist specifically to protect sensitive information from being shared inappropriately.

## Conclusion

Whether in legal, professional, or personal domains, the concept of disclosure underscores the importance of honesty and transparency in fostering trust. Understanding when, what, and how to disclose information is a nuanced skill that requires balancing openness with discretion, ultimately shaping the integrity of relationships and institutions alike.

counterfactuals.output:
# Provisional Patent Disclosure

## Title of Invention
**System and Method for Adaptive Luminaire Brightness Control Using Mobile Device Ambient Light Sensing and Distance Estimation**

---

## Field of the Invention

This disclosure relates to smart lighting systems, and more particularly to a method and apparatus for dynamically adjusting the brightness of a networked luminaire based on distance estimation derived from ambient light sensor readings obtained from a companion mobile computing device (e.g., smartphone, tablet, or wearable).

---

## Background

Conventional smart lighting systems (e.g., Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected bulbs) allow brightness adjustment via manual user input through a mobile application, voice assistant, or preset schedule. These systems do not automatically account for the user's physical distance from the light source, which significantly affects perceived illuminance at the point of use.

Existing proximity-based lighting solutions typically rely on:
- **Fixed motion/PIR sensors** — detect presence but not distance or precise position relative to the lamp
- **Bluetooth RSSI-based proximity estimation** — coarse-grained, susceptible to interference and multipath signal errors
- **Camera-based computer vision** — computationally expensive and raises privacy concerns

There exists a need for a low-cost, privacy-preserving, computationally lightweight method to estimate the distance between a user and a light source using hardware already present on nearly all modern smartphones — namely, the ambient light sensor (ALS) — in order to enable automatic, physiologically appropriate brightness adjustment without requiring additional dedicated hardware.

---

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention discloses a system wherein:

1. A **luminaire** (lamp, fixture, or bulb) is equipped with wireless communication capability (e.g., Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, Zigbee) and a controllable driver circuit for adjusting output brightness.
2. A **mobile device application** running on a user's smartphone continuously or periodically samples the device's built-in ambient light sensor.
3. The system establishes a **calibrated relationship** between (a) the known, commanded output brightness of the luminaire, (b) the ambient light sensor's real-time lux reading, and (c) the inverse-square-law attenuation of light intensity with distance, to compute an **estimated distance** between the user's device and the light source.
4. Based on this estimated distance and a **target illuminance level** (either user-specified, derived from a lighting profile, or determined by ambient conditions, time of day, or activity mode), the system computes an **adjusted brightness command** and transmits it to the luminaire's controller.
5. The process operates in a **continuous feedback loop**, allowing brightness to adapt in real time as the user moves closer to or farther from the light source, while compensating for known confounding variables (see below).

---

## Detailed Description

### 1. System Architecture

The system comprises three primary components:

**A. Luminaire Module**
- Light-emitting element (LED array, CFL, etc.)
- Dimmable driver circuit responsive to PWM or analog control signal
- Wireless communication transceiver (BLE/Wi-Fi/Zigbee/Thread)
- Local microcontroller storing a device ID, calibration profile, and current commanded brightness state
- Optional onboard reference photosensor for self-calibration (see Alternative Embodiments)

**B. Mobile Device Application**
- Software module interfacing with the device's native ambient light sensor API
- Distance estimation engine (described in Section 2)
- User interface for setting target illuminance, lighting "scenes," or activity-based presets (reading, relaxing, working)
- Wireless communication stack to pair with and transmit commands to the luminaire

**C. Control/Calibration Server (Optional Cloud Component)**
- Stores per-device calibration curves
- Aggregates learned environmental correction factors (e.g., typical ambient light contribution in a given room, reflectance coefficients)
- Facilitates multi-luminaire disambiguation in rooms with more than one smart light

---

### 2. Distance Estimation Method

The core inventive method estimates distance **d** between the smartphone and the luminaire using the following process:

**Step 1 — Baseline Calibration**
During an initial setup routine, the user holds the smartphone at a known, fixed distance (e.g., arm's length, or a distance measured via the phone's camera-based AR depth API or LiDAR sensor if available) from the luminaire while the luminaire cycles through a series of known brightness levels (B₁, B₂, ... Bₙ). The corresponding lux readings (L₁, L₂, ... Lₙ) from the ambient light sensor are recorded, establishing a **device- and environment-specific calibration curve**:

  L = k · B / d²  (inverse square approximation)

where **k** is an empirically derived proportionality constant accounting for luminaire luminous efficacy, sensor sensitivity, and diffusion/reflectance losses.

**Step 2 — Ambient Baseline Subtraction**
Prior to or during calibration, the system samples ambient light levels with the luminaire OFF, establishing an ambient offset **L_ambient**. This value is continuously updated during system idle periods (e.g., using periodic brief blackout pulses, imperceptible flicker sampling, or correlation with a smartphone camera exposure metric) to compensate for time-of-day and external light source changes (sunlight, other lamps).

**Step 3 — Real-Time Distance Computation**
During operation, with the luminaire at known commanded brightness **B_current**, the mobile device continuously samples lux value **L_measured**. The corrected contribution from the luminaire is:

  L_lamp = L_measured − L_ambient

The estimated distance is then computed as:

  d_estimated = √(k · B_current / L_lamp)

**Step 4 — Noise Filtering & Smoothing**
Raw distance estimates are passed through a smoothing filter (e.g., Kalman filter or exponential moving average) to reduce jitter caused by sensor noise, hand movement, or transient occlusions (e.g., the phone screen facing away from the lamp).

**Step 5 — Multi-Sample Disambiguation (Optional)**
Where multiple luminaires are present, each luminaire is assigned a unique, imperceptible modulation signature (e.g., high-frequency PWM dithering or a coded flicker pattern below human perceptual threshold) so the mobile device can attribute lux contributions to a specific source using lock-in-style demodulation or correlation detection.

---

### 3. Brightness Adjustment Logic

Once **d_estimated** is computed, the system determines the required luminaire output **B_target** to achieve a desired illuminance **L_target** at the user's location:

  B_target = (L_target · d_estimated²) / k

This value is transmitted to the luminaire controller, which adjusts its PWM duty cycle or driver current accordingly. The control loop may include:

- **Deadband/hysteresis logic** to prevent flicker from minor distance fluctuations
- **Rate limiting** to ensure gradual, perceptually smooth brightness transitions
- **Activity-based target profiles** (e.g., higher lux for reading, lower for ambient relaxation) selectable by the user or inferred from device usage patterns (screen-on state, app in foreground, accelerometer-detected stillness)
- **Multi-user arbitration logic** when multiple devices are paired to a single luminaire (e.g., average, nearest-user-priority, or manual override modes)

---

### 4. Alternative Embodiments

1. **Onboard Reference Photosensor**: The luminaire itself includes a fixed photosensor for self-calibration, reducing dependency on manual calibration steps and enabling the system to compensate for bulb aging/dimming over its lifespan.

2. **Camera-Assisted Depth Fusion**: On devices equipped with LiDAR, structured light, or stereo depth cameras, depth data may be fused with ALS-derived estimates via sensor fusion (e.g., Kalman/particle filter) to improve accuracy, using the ALS method as a fallback when camera-based depth is unavailable or the device is in-pocket.

3. **Wearable Implementation**: The ambient light sensor of a smartwatch or fitness band is used in place of, or in conjunction with, a smartphone sensor, useful for hands-free operation.

4. **Multi-Lamp Room Mapping**: The system builds a spatial map of multiple luminaires in a room using triangulated distance estimates from a single moving device over time, enabling coordinated group dimming (e.g., a "spotlight follows user" effect).

5. **Color Temperature Adjustment**: The same distance-estimation pipeline is extended to adjust correlated color temperature (CCT) in addition to brightness, based on distance-dependent perceptual color rendering models.

6. **Battery/Privacy-Conscious Mode**: Low-power operation mode samples ALS at reduced frequency and disables when device is in-pocket (detected via proximity sensor) or screen-off for extended periods, resuming full-rate sampling upon wake.

---

### 5. Advantages Over Prior Art

- Utilizes **existing smartphone hardware** (ambient light sensor) — no additional wearable, beacon, or camera hardware required
- **Privacy-preserving**: does not rely on camera imagery or facial/body recognition
- **Low computational overhead** compared to computer-vision-based proximity systems
- Provides **continuous, real-time** adjustment rather than discrete zone-based triggering (as with PIR/motion sensors)
- Compensates for **ambient light and multi-source interference** through baseline subtraction and modulation-based signal disambiguation
- Scalable to **multi-luminaire, multi-user environments**

---

## Claims (Illustrative/Non-Limiting)

1. A method for adjusting the brightness of a luminaire, comprising: receiving, at a mobile computing device, an ambient light sensor reading; determining a known current brightness setting of the luminaire; computing an estimated distance between the mobile computing device and the luminaire based on the ambient light sensor reading, the known current brightness setting, and a stored calibration relationship; and transmitting an updated brightness command to the luminaire based on the estimated distance and a target illuminance value.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein the calibration relationship is derived from an inverse-square-law model relating luminous intensity, distance, and sensor-reported illuminance.

3. The method of claim 1, further comprising subtracting an ambient light baseline value, measured independently of the luminaire's output, from the ambient light sensor reading prior to computing the estimated distance.

4. The method of claim 1, further comprising applying a smoothing filter to a plurality of sequential distance estimates to reduce measurement noise prior to transmitting the updated brightness command.

5. The method of claim 1, wherein the luminaire emits a unique modulation signature enabling the mobile computing device to disambiguate its light contribution from that of one or more additional luminaires.

6. The method of claim 1, wherein the target illuminance value is determined based on a user-selected activity profile.

7. A system comprising: a luminaire having a wireless communication module and a controllable brightness driver; a mobile computing device comprising an ambient light sensor and a wireless communication module; and a processor configured to execute the method of claim 1.

8. The system of claim 7, further comprising a fixed reference photosensor integrated into the luminaire, configured to provide self-calibration data compensating for luminaire output degradation over time.

9. The system of claim 7, wherein the mobile computing device further comprises a depth-sensing camera, and wherein the processor is further configured to fuse depth camera data with the ambient-light-sensor-derived distance estimate to produce a refined distance estimate.

10. A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by a processor, cause performance of the method of claim 1.

---

## Drawings (Descriptions for Attached Fig

# PATENT ABSTRACT

**LIGHTING ARRANGEMENT WITH DISTANCE-DETERMINING FUNCTIONALITY BASED ON LUMINOUS OUTPUT CALIBRATION**

A lighting arrangement configured to determine the distance between a light source and a mobile device is disclosed. The arrangement comprises a lighting device having at least one light-emitting element configured to emit a luminous output at a known or controllable intensity; a communication module configured to establish wireless communication with the mobile device and receive measurement data indicative of a luminous output intensity sensed by the mobile device; a calibration data storage configured to store calibration data correlating luminous output intensity values with corresponding reference distances; and a controller operatively coupled to the light-emitting element, the communication module, and the calibration data storage. The controller is configured to control the light-emitting element to emit the luminous output according to a predetermined or known emission parameter, receive, via the communication module, the measurement data representing the luminous output intensity as measured by a light sensor of the mobile device, retrieve the calibration data from the calibration data storage, and determine a distance between the lighting device and the mobile device by comparing the received measurement data with the calibration data. The lighting arrangement enables accurate, cost-effective localization and/or proximity detection of mobile devices without requiring additional dedicated ranging hardware.

---

# EXEMPLARY CLAIMS

**Claim 1** (Independent — System Claim)

A lighting arrangement for determining a distance to a mobile device, the lighting arrangement comprising:

a) a lighting device comprising at least one light-emitting element configured to emit a luminous output;

b) a communication module configured to communicate wirelessly with the mobile device;

c) a calibration data storage configured to store calibration data, the calibration data correlating a plurality of luminous output intensity values with corresponding known distances between the lighting device and a reference sensor position; and

d) a controller operatively coupled to the light-emitting element, the communication module, and the calibration data storage, the controller configured to:
   i. control the light-emitting element to emit the luminous output at a determined emission intensity;
   ii. receive, via the communication module, measurement data from the mobile device, the measurement data representative of the luminous output intensity as measured by a light sensor of the mobile device;
   iii. retrieve the calibration data from the calibration data storage; and
   iv. determine a distance between the lighting device and the mobile device based on a comparison of the measurement data with the retrieved calibration data.

**Claim 2** (Dependent)

The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the controller is further configured to adjust the emission intensity of the light-emitting element based on ambient light conditions detected via the communication module, and to update the calibration data storage accordingly.

**Claim 3** (Dependent)

The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the communication module is configured to transmit an identifier associated with the determined emission intensity to the mobile device, such that the mobile device associates the measured luminous output intensity with the identifier prior to transmitting the measurement data.

**Claim 4** (Dependent)

The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the calibration data comprises a lookup table or a mathematical function relating luminous flux, distance, and ambient light attenuation coefficients.

**Claim 5** (Dependent)

The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the controller is further configured to determine a position of the mobile device within an illuminated area based on the determined distance and distances determined for the mobile device relative to at least one additional lighting device.

**Claim 6** (Independent — Method Claim)

A method for determining a distance between a lighting device and a mobile device, the method comprising:

emitting, via a light-emitting element of the lighting device, a luminous output at a controlled emission intensity;

receiving, via a communication module, measurement data from the mobile device representative of the luminous output intensity as sensed by the mobile device;

retrieving, from a calibration data storage, calibration data correlating luminous output intensity values with corresponding distances; and

determining, via a controller, the distance between the lighting device and the mobile device based on a comparison between the received measurement data and the retrieved calibration data.

---

*Note: This document is a template/exemplary abstract and claim set drafted for illustrative purposes. Actual patent prosecution requires review by a registered patent attorney or agent to ensure claims are properly scoped, novel, non-obvious, and compliant with jurisdiction-specific requirements (e.g., USPTO, EPO). Prior art search and specification drafting (including detailed description, drawings, and enablement support) would be required to support these claims in a real filing.*

# Patent Application Draft

## TITLE OF THE INVENTION
System and Method for Distance-Based Automatic Brightness Adjustment of a Dimmable Lighting Device Using Mobile Device Calibration Data

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to lighting control systems, and more particularly to a dimmable lighting device configured to communicate with a mobile computing device, wherein calibration data correlating measured light intensity to distance is utilized to enable automatic adjustment of brightness output.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Conventional dimmable lighting systems typically require manual adjustment via physical controls, switches, or software interfaces, without accounting for the spatial relationship between the light source and a user or target device. Existing ambient light sensing solutions often fail to correlate sensor readings with an accurate distance metric, resulting in imprecise or non-responsive brightness control. There exists a need for a system that dynamically calibrates the relationship between light intensity and distance, thereby enabling automatic, context-aware brightness adjustments without requiring manual user intervention.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with one embodiment, the present invention provides a lighting system comprising a dimmable lighting device and a mobile computing device configured for wireless communication therewith. The mobile computing device includes a light sensor configured to measure ambient light intensity emitted by the lighting device at varying distances. A calibration module, which may reside on the mobile device, the lighting device, a remote server, or a combination thereof, generates and stores calibration data correlating measured light intensity values to corresponding distance values.

During operation, the system utilizes the stored calibration data to estimate a real-time distance between the mobile computing device and the lighting device based on a currently measured light intensity value. A control module then automatically adjusts a brightness output level of the lighting device based on the estimated distance, according to a predetermined or user-configurable brightness profile.

In some embodiments, the calibration data is generated through an initial calibration routine in which the lighting device emits light at one or more known intensity levels while the mobile device is positioned at one or more known or measured distances, and the resulting sensor readings are recorded and associated with the corresponding distances to form a calibration curve, lookup table, or predictive model.

---

In an exemplary calibration process, illustrated in **FIG. 2**, the system generates calibration data as follows:

Referring to **FIG. 3**, during a runtime operational mode, the system performs automatic brightness adjustment as follows:

2. The control application 126 accesses the stored calibration data and applies the measured value Iₓ thereto, in order to estimate a corresponding current distance value, Dₓ, between the mobile computing device 120 and the lighting device 110.
3. The control application 126, or alternatively a control module resident on the lighting device 110, determines a target brightness level based on the estimated distance Dₓ, in accordance with a predetermined brightness profile. Such profile may specify, for example, that brightness output should increase as distance increases (to maintain a substantially constant perceived illumination level), decrease as distance increases, or follow a user-defined custom relationship.
4. A brightness adjustment command corresponding to the target brightness level is transmitted via the communication link 130 to the lighting device 110.
5. The processor 114 of the lighting device 110 executes the brightness adjustment command by modulating the dimming circuit 112 to achieve the target brightness output level.

In some embodiments, steps 1–5 are performed continuously or at periodic intervals, thereby enabling dynamic, real-time brightness adjustment responsive to changes in the relative position of the mobile computing device 120.

In an alternative embodiment, the roles of measurement and control may be distributed differently among the system components; for example, the lighting device 110 itself may include a light sensor configured to detect reflected or ambient light correlated to the position of the mobile computing device 120, without departing from the scope of the invention.

In another embodiment, the calibration data may be dynamically updated over time based on accumulated usage data, environmental changes, or user feedback, using an adaptive or machine-learning-based algorithm.

In yet another embodiment, the system supports multiple mobile computing devices 120a, 120b, ... 120n, and/or multiple lighting devices 110a, 110b, ... 110n, wherein calibration data is generated and applied on a per-device or per-pairing basis, and wherein brightness adjustment logic accounts for the aggregate or relative positioning of multiple devices within an environment.

# PATENT DISCLOSURE

## TITLE OF INVENTION
**LIGHTING CONTROL SYSTEM WITH MOBILE DEVICE FEEDBACK AND DISTANCE-BASED CALIBRATION FOR ADAPTIVE LUMINOUS OUTPUT REGULATION**

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to lighting control systems, and more particularly to a system and method for dynamically adjusting luminous output of a lighting fixture based on light measurements received from a mobile communication device, using distance-dependent calibration data stored in a memory associated with the lighting control system.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Conventional lighting control systems typically rely on fixed-position ambient light sensors integrated into the luminaire housing or mounted at a stationary location within a room. These systems suffer from several limitations:

1. **Positional Rigidity**: Fixed sensors measure light intensity only at their installed location, which may not correspond to the location where illumination is actually needed (e.g., a desk surface, reading area, or task location).

2. **Lack of Distance Compensation**: Existing systems generally do not account for the variable distance between the light source and the point of measurement, leading to inaccurate output adjustments when the measurement point changes relative to the fixture.

3. **Limited User Interaction**: Users have limited ability to provide real-time, location-specific feedback to the lighting system regarding perceived or measured illumination levels at their specific location.

4. **Calibration Deficiencies**: Prior art systems do not adequately compensate for the inverse-square relationship (or empirically-derived attenuation profile) between luminous intensity and distance, resulting in either overcorrection or undercorrection of light output.

There exists a need for a lighting control system that leverages ubiquitous mobile communication devices—already equipped with ambient light sensors and camera sensors—as a distributed, mobile light-measurement input, combined with stored calibration data that accounts for the distance between the mobile device and the light source, to achieve accurate and responsive luminous output control.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure describes a lighting control system comprising:

- A **lighting fixture** having one or more adjustable light-emitting elements (e.g., LED arrays) with a controllable driver circuit;
- A **communication module** configured to establish wireless communication (e.g., Bluetooth, Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, Zigbee, NFC, or cellular) with a mobile communication device;
- A **mobile communication device** (e.g., smartphone, tablet, wearable) equipped with a light sensor (ambient light sensor, camera-based photometric sensor, or equivalent), configured to measure incident light intensity at its current location and transmit the measurement data to the lighting control system;
- A **distance determination module** configured to estimate or receive the distance between the mobile communication device and the lighting fixture, using one or more of: received signal strength indication (RSSI), time-of-flight (ToF) ranging, ultra-wideband (UWB) positioning, camera-based depth estimation, or user-input/manual entry;
- A **memory/storage module** containing pre-stored **calibration data** correlating expected luminous output, sensor-measured light intensity, and distance between the fixture and measurement point;
- A **control processor** configured to:
  1. Receive the light measurement data and distance data from the mobile communication device;
  2. Retrieve corresponding calibration data from memory based on the determined distance;
  3. Compute a target luminous output adjustment based on a comparison between the received light measurement, the calibration data, and a desired illumination setpoint;
  4. Transmit a control signal to the lighting fixture driver to adjust the luminous output (intensity, color temperature, or both) accordingly.

This architecture enables **closed-loop, distance-compensated illumination control** using the mobile device as a portable photometric probe, improving accuracy of light delivery at the user's actual point of need rather than at a fixed sensor location.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. System Architecture Overview

Referring to the general system architecture, the lighting control system (100) comprises the following primary subsystems:

**(A) Lighting Fixture Unit (110)**
- Light-emitting element array (111) — LED, OLED, or other solid-state emitters, optionally multi-channel (e.g., warm/cool white or RGBW) to support tunable color temperature;
- Driver circuit (112) — provides pulse-width modulation (PWM) or analog current control to the emitter array in response to control signals;
- Local controller/microcontroller (113) — processes commands received from the central control processor or operates as an integrated control unit;
- Wireless communication module (114) — supports bidirectional communication with the mobile communication device and/or a central hub.

**(B) Mobile Communication Device (120)**
- Ambient light sensor (121) and/or camera module (122) capable of capturing luminance/illuminance data;
- Companion application (123) executing on the device's processor, configured to:
  - Sample light sensor data at defined intervals or upon user initiation;
  - Package sensor data with a timestamp and (optionally) device orientation data from an integrated IMU (accelerometer/gyroscope/magnetometer);
  - Transmit the data packet to the lighting control system via the wireless communication module (124).

**(C) Distance Determination Module (130)**
The distance between the mobile communication device (120) and the lighting fixture (110) is determined by one or more of the following methods:
  - **RSSI-based estimation**: Signal attenuation between the fixture's wireless transceiver and the mobile device is measured and converted to an estimated distance using a pre-characterized path-loss model.
  - **Time-of-Flight (ToF) / UWB ranging**: Dedicated ranging radios in both the fixture and mobile device compute precise distance via round-trip signal timing.
  - **Camera-based depth/proximity estimation**: The mobile device's camera captures an image of the fixture (or a fiducial marker/QR code on the fixture), and the system computes distance based on known fixture dimensions and image scale.
  - **Manual/user input**: The user manually inputs or confirms an approximate distance via the companion application interface.

**(D) Calibration Data Storage (140)**
A non-volatile memory (140), located either within the lighting fixture's local controller, within a central hub, or in cloud-based storage accessible by the control processor, stores a calibration table or function of the form:

```
CalibrationData(d) = { L_expected(d, P) , SensorResponse(d, P) }
```

where:
- `d` = distance between mobile device and fixture,
- `P` = luminous output power setting of the fixture (e.g., PWM duty cycle or drive current),
- `L_expected(d, P)` = expected illuminance at distance `d` for a given output setting `P`, derived empirically during a factory or field calibration procedure,
- `SensorResponse(d, P)` = expected mobile device sensor reading (accounting for sensor gain, spectral response, and device-specific correction factors) at distance `d` for output setting `P`.

This calibration data may be generated via:
- Factory calibration using a reference photometric instrument at multiple distances and output levels;
- Field/self-calibration routines wherein the user is guided to place the mobile device at known reference distances (e.g., using AR-guided distance markers) while the system cycles through output levels and records sensor responses.

**(E) Control Processor (150)**
The control processor may reside within the lighting fixture, within a separate hub/gateway device, or be distributed across the mobile device's companion application and the fixture's local controller. Its functions include:
  1. **Data Reception**: Receive light measurement `M_received` and distance `d` from the mobile device.
  2. **Calibration Lookup/Interpolation**: Query the calibration data store for the expected sensor response `SensorResponse(d, P_current)` at the current output setting and the measured distance. If the exact distance is not present in the stored table, perform interpolation (linear, spline, or polynomial) between the nearest stored calibration points.
  3. **Error Computation**: Compute a deviation/error signal:
     ```
     ΔE = M_target - (M_received × CorrectionFactor(d))
     ```
     where `M_target` is the desired illuminance setpoint (user-defined or context-derived), and `CorrectionFactor(d)` normalizes the raw sensor reading to account for distance-dependent attenuation and sensor characteristics as derived from calibration data.
  4. **Output Adjustment Calculation**: Using a control algorithm (e.g., proportional-integral (PI) controller, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, or lookup-table-driven step adjustment), compute a new output setting `P_new`:
     ```
     P_new = P_current + K_p·ΔE + K_i·∫ΔE dt
     ```
  5. **Command Transmission**: Transmit updated drive command to the fixture's driver circuit (112) to adjust luminous flux and/or color temperature.
  6. **Iterative Feedback Loop**: Repeat the measurement-adjustment cycle at defined intervals, upon detected movement of the mobile device (via IMU or distance-change detection), or upon user request, to maintain the desired illumination level as ambient conditions or user position change.

### 2. Distance-Dependent Calibration Methodology

A key inventive aspect is the use of **distance as an explicit input variable** in the calibration and correction process, rather than treating sensor readings as distance-agnostic. The calibration data may be structured as a two-dimensional or three-dimensional lookup table indexed by distance and output power, or may be represented as a parametric function (e.g., modified inverse-square law with empirically fitted attenuation coefficients):

```
E(d) = (I₀ / d²) × k_atten(d) + E_ambient
```

where:
- `I₀` = luminous intensity of the fixture at reference output setting,
- `k_atten(d)` = empirically-derived attenuation correction coefficient (accounting for beam angle, diffusion, obstructions, or fixture-specific optical characteristics that deviate from ideal inverse-square behavior),
- `E_ambient` = ambient/background light contribution, which may be separately estimated by sampling sensor data with the fixture output temporarily set to zero or minimum.

This function or its tabulated equivalent is stored persistently and referenced during runtime operation, allowing the system to disambiguate whether a low sensor reading is attributable to (a) genuine insufficient fixture output, (b) increased distance between fixture and mobile device, or (c) low ambient contribution—and adjust its correction accordingly.

### 3. Operational Flow (Exemplary Method Claim Basis)

**Step 1**: Establish wireless communication pairing between the lighting fixture (or associated hub) and the mobile communication device.

**Step 2**: Mobile device's companion application activates onboard light sensor and (optionally) initiates distance-determination procedure (RSSI, ToF, camera-based, or manual).

**Step 3**: Mobile device transmits light measurement data and distance data to the lighting control system's communication module.

**Step 4**: Control processor retrieves relevant calibration data from stored memory corresponding to the received (or interpolated) distance value.

**Step 5**: Control processor computes corrected illuminance estimate by applying calibration-derived correction factor to raw sensor measurement.

**Step 6**: Control processor compares corrected illuminance estimate to target setpoint and computes required adjustment to luminous output.

**Step 7**: Control processor transmits adjustment command to lighting fixture driver circuit.

**Step 8**: Lighting fixture adjusts luminous output accordingly (intensity and/or color temperature).

**Step 9**: Process repeats iteratively, optionally triggered by: (a) periodic timer, (b) detected change in mobile device position/distance exceeding a threshold, (c) detected change in ambient

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to smart lighting systems, and more particularly to an adaptive illumination control apparatus that infers spatial distance parameters from measured luminous output characteristics to autonomously regulate light intensity without requiring dedicated distance-sensing hardware.

## Background

Conventional smart lighting systems typically rely on discrete proximity sensors, ultrasonic rangefinders, infrared time-of-flight modules, or camera-based depth estimation to determine the distance between a light source and a target surface or occupant. These approaches introduce additional hardware cost, increased power consumption, susceptibility to environmental interference, and mechanical complexity. There exists a need for a lighting control system capable of estimating distance-related parameters using only luminous output measurements already available within the lighting apparatus, thereby simplifying system architecture while preserving adaptive control functionality.

## Summary

In accordance with the present invention, a smart lighting system is provided comprising a **controller**, a **calibration database**, and a **wireless communication module**, cooperatively configured to infer an unknown distance parameter from measured luminous output and to adjust light output accordingly.

In one embodiment, the system includes:

1. **A light-emitting element** configured to emit illumination at a controllable intensity level and further configured to report, or be associated with, one or more photometric sensors that measure a resulting luminous output value at a receiving surface or associated photodetector.

2. **A calibration database**, stored in a non-transitory memory accessible to the controller, containing a plurality of reference data points correlating known distances to corresponding luminous output measurements obtained under one or more predetermined emission intensities. The calibration database may be populated during a factory calibration process, a field commissioning procedure, or through iterative learning during runtime operation, and may further account for variables such as ambient light contribution, reflectance characteristics of the target surface, and emitter aging characteristics.

3. **A controller**, operatively coupled to the light-emitting element and the calibration database, configured to:
   - receive a measured luminous output value corresponding to a current emission intensity;
   - query the calibration database to identify a correlation between the measured luminous output value and a corresponding distance value, using interpolation, curve-fitting, or a trained regression/inference model derived from the calibration data;
   - compute an inferred distance value representing the estimated separation between the light-emitting element and a target surface or object, absent any direct distance-sensing hardware;
   - determine an adjusted light output level based on the inferred distance value and one or more control parameters (e.g., a desired illuminance target, energy-saving policy, or user-defined preference); and
   - transmit a control signal to modulate the light-emitting element to the adjusted light output level.

4. **A wireless communication module**, coupled to the controller, configured to transmit and receive data including calibration updates, measured luminous output values from remote or networked sensor nodes, inferred distance values, control commands, and/or firmware updates. The wireless communication module may support communication protocols including, without limitation, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, Thread, or proprietary RF protocols, thereby enabling the controller to coordinate operation among a plurality of networked lighting fixtures and to receive supplemental calibration data from a remote server or cloud-based calibration service.

In certain embodiments, the controller further comprises a feedback loop wherein subsequent luminous output measurements, taken after adjustment of the light output level, are used to refine the calibration database in real time, thereby improving the accuracy of future distance inferences and compensating for environmental drift, surface reflectance variation, or component aging.

In further embodiments, the system may incorporate multiple light-emitting elements and/or multiple photometric sensors disposed at different locations, wherein the controller aggregates a plurality of luminous output measurements and corresponding calibration data to derive a distance map or spatial distribution estimate, enabling zone-based or object-specific illumination control.

## Advantages

The disclosed system advantageously eliminates the need for dedicated proximity or distance-sensing hardware, reduces component cost and power consumption, and enables retrofit deployment into existing luminaire housings. The use of a calibration database in conjunction with wireless connectivity further enables distributed learning across a fleet of networked lighting devices, improving inference accuracy over time and across diverse installation environments.

## Brief Description of Alternative Embodiments

It will be understood by those skilled in the art that the calibration database may be implemented as a lookup table, a parametric model (e.g., inverse-square law approximation with correction coefficients), or a machine-learning model such as a neural network or Gaussian process regressor trained on historical luminous output and distance data. It will further be understood that the wireless communication module may facilitate integration with home automation systems, building management systems, or Internet-of-Things (IoT) platforms, and that the controller may be implemented as a microcontroller, application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), field-programmable gate array (FPGA), or distributed cloud-based processing system, without departing from the scope of the invention as defined by the appended claims.
